title: Applications of machine learning to machine fault diagnosis: A
introduction:
21
Fault diagnosis serves an important role in pursuing the relationship between the monitoring
22
data and the health states of machines [1, 2], which has been a widely concerned issue in
23
Page 4
machine health management. Traditionally, the relationship is caught by abundant experience
1
and huge expert knowledge of engineers. For example, an experienced engineer is able to
2
diagnose the faults of engines depending on the abnormal sound or locate the bearing faults by
3
using advanced signal processing methods to analyze the vibration signals. In engineering
4
scenarios, however, the machine users would like an automatic method to shorten the
5
maintenance cycle and improve the diagnosis accuracy. In particular, with the help of artificial
6
intelligence, the procedure of fault diagnosis is expected to be intelligent enough to
7
automatically detect and recognize the health states of machines [2-5].
8
Intelligent fault diagnosis (IFD) refers to applications of machine learning theories, such as
9
artificial neural networks (ANN), support vector machine (SVM), and deep neural networks
10
(DNN), to machine fault diagnosis [6, 7], which is promising to achieve the above purpose. This
11
kind of methods uses machine learning theories to adaptively learn the diagnosis knowledge of
12
machines from the collected data instead of utilizing the experience and knowledge of
13
engineers. Specifically, IFD aims to construct diagnosis models that are able to automatically
14
bridge the relationship between the collected data and the health states of machines.
15
In recent years, IFD has attracted much attention from academic researchers and industrial
16
engineers, which deeply relates to the development of machine learning [6-9]. We count the
17
number of publications about IFD based on the search results from the Web of Science, which is
18
shown in Fig. 1. According to the results on the topic of machine fault diagnosis by using
19
machine learning, the number of publications has rapidly increased since the 2010s. Therefore,
20
we roughly divide the research of IFD into three periods as follows.
21
Page 5

2
1) In the past, traditional machine learning theories were popularly conducted in IFD from the
3
debut to the 2010s. The early research of machine learning derived back to the 1950s, and
4
boosted to be an important interest of artificial intelligence in the 1980s [10]. A number of
5
traditional theories were invented during this period such as ANN [11], SVM [12], k-Nearest
6
Neighbor (kNN) [13], and probabilistic graphical model (PGM) [14]. These theories promoted
7
Page 6
the emergence of IFD including expert system-based approaches [15], ANN-based approaches
1
[16], SVM-based approaches [17], and other intelligent approaches [7]. In these approaches, the
2
features were artificially extracted from the collected data. After that, the sensitive features were
3
selected to train diagnosis models that could automatically recognize the health states of
4
machines. With the help of traditional machine learning, the diagnosis models began to establish
5
the relationship between the selected features and the health states of machines, which
6
weakened the contribution of human labor in machine fault diagnosis and pushed it into the era
7
of artificial intelligence.
8
2) In the present, deep learning theories have come to reform IFD since the 2010s [18].
9
Although IFD in the past is able to recognize the health sates of machines instead of the fault
10
inspection by humans, the artificial feature extraction still mostly depends on the human labor.
11
Furthermore, traditional machine learning theories are not applicable to the increasingly-grown
12
data because of the low generalization performance, which reduces the diagnosis accuracy. Deep
13
learning is a new topic in the field of machine learning, which could date back to the research of
14
neural networks in the 1980s [19, 20], such as autoencoders (AE) [21] and the restricted
15
Boltzmann machine (RBM) [22]. This topic has been widely concerned since 2006 when Hinton
16
[23] used the greedy layer-wise pre-training strategy to train the deep belief network (DBN). In
17
addition, convolutional neural network (CNN) also made a series of breakthroughs, such as
18
AlexNet [24] and ResNet [25]. These theories further inspired the development of IFD and
19
induced a number of achievements [4, 6-9] including stacked AE-based approaches, DBN-based
20
approaches, CNN-based approaches, and ResNet-based approaches. In the approaches, deep
21
learning helps automatically learn fault features from the collected data instead of the artificial
22
feature extraction in the past period of IFD. They attempt to provide end-to-end diagnosis
23
Page 7
models when handling the increasingly-grown data. The models are expected to directly connect
1
the raw monitoring data to their corresponding health states of machines, which further releases
2
the contribution of human labor in IFD.
3
3) In the future, transfer learning theories will promote the research of IFD in engineering
4
scenarios. Although deep learning has achieved significant successes in machine fault diagnosis
5
currently, the successes are subject to a common assumption that there are sufficient labeled data
6
to train diagnosis models. However, such assumption is unpractical in engineering scenarios due
7
to two main reasons [26]. First, machines usually work with the healthy condition, and faults
8
seldom happen. As a result, a considerable number of healthy data are collected, while faulty
9
data are insufficient. Second, it takes huge cost to acquire the machine health states
10
corresponding to the collected data, i.e., labeling the data. Consequently, majority of collected
11
data are unlabeled in engineering scenarios. For the above reasons, the collected data are
12
insufficient to train reliable diagnosis models. Fortunately, transfer learning is concerned to
13
overcome such weaknesses by applying the knowledge learned from one or multiple tasks to
14
other related but novel ones [27]. This theory derives back to 1995 in a different name of the
15
learning to learn [28], and has got some achievements since the 2010s, such as transfer
16
component analysis (TCA) [29], joint distribution adaptation (JDA) [30], and TrAdaboost [31].
17
After that, it has been developed with the help of deep learning theories since 2015 and yielded
18
some achievements in the field of computer vision [32], such as transfer denoising autoencoder
19
(TDA) [33] and joint adaptation network (JAN) [34]. In the field of IFD, some researchers have
20
begun to develop a few studies generally including feature-based approaches [26], generative
21
adversarial network (GAN) based approaches [35], instance-based approaches [36], and
22
parameter-based approaches [37]. These approaches are expected to provide diagnosis models
23
Page 8
that could transfer the diagnosis knowledge learned from one or multiple diagnosis tasks to
1
realize other related but different diagnosis ones. Therefore, transfer-learning theories are
2
expected to overcome the problems of lacking labeled samples and finally enlarge the
3
applications of IFD in engineering scenarios.
4
To summarize the research of IFD, Liu et al. [7] briefly reviewed the applications of artificial
5
intelligence for fault diagnosis of rotating machines, and mainly focused on applications of
6
traditional machine learning. Khan et al [8] presented categories of the artificial intelligence-
7
based methods in system health management, and further reviewed the applications of deep
8
learning. Duan et al. [6] and Zhao et al. [9] reviewed the commonly-used deep learning theories
9
and the applications to machine fault diagnosis. Hoang et al. [4] provided a review about
10
applications of deep learning to bearing fault diagnosis. However, these reviews have three
11
shortcomings. 1) The previous reviews just concerned IFD in a certain period like using
12
traditional machine learning or using deep learning. For example, Ref. [7] mainly focused on the
13
applications of traditional machine learning, and Ref. [4, 6, 8, 9] just reviewed applications of
14
deep learning to machine fault diagnosis. As a result, a review to systematically cover the
15
development of IFD from the past to the future is still left blank. 2) These reviews have not
16
reported a roadmap on IFD to predict future trends yet. But for review papers, the readers prefer
17
to be interested in potential trends of IFD in the next five or ten years. 3) They just cover the
18
publications of IFD before 2017. In recent years, however, the number of publications has
19
rapidly increased every year. As shown in Fig. 1, the number of publications from 2017 to 2019
20
almost approaches to the total of that before 2017. Therefore, it needs a new review to summary
21
the current research progress of IFD.
22
In order to overcome aforementioned shortcomings, this paper systematically reviews the
23
Page 9
development of IFD and pictures a roadmap for this field. The contributions of this review are
1
refined as follows. 1) The development of IFD is summarized into three periods. In the past,
2
traditional machine learning was expected to lead machine fault diagnosis into the era of
3
artificial intelligence. In the present, deep learning focuses on further enhanced benefits in IFD.
4
In the future, transfer learning is viewed as a future prospect to promote the applications of IFD
5
to engineering scenarios, and we try to cautiously detail them following the issues of “why to
6
transfer”, “what is transfer”, and “how to transfer”. 2) A roadmap of IFD is pictured in this
7
review. The roadmap includes potential research trends and provides valuable guideline for
8
researchers over the future works.
9
The rest of this review is organized as follows. In Section 2, we focus on the development of
10
IFD in the past including applications of traditional machine learning theories. Section 3 reviews
11
the applications of deep learning theories, which are considered as the present period in the
12
development of IFD. Section 4 argues applications of transfer learning to IFD including the
13
motivation, the definitions, and some exploratory works. In Section 5, we further display a
14
roadmap when combined with the challenges of IFD. Conclusions are enclosed in Section 6.
15
2. Past: IFD using traditional machine learning theories
16
This section includes the motivation about applications of traditional machine learning
17
theories, and further reviews IFD in the past according to a commonly-implemented diagnosis
18
process including data collection, artificial feature extraction, and health state recognition.
19
2.1. Overview
20
Traditionally, the process of fault diagnosis is mostly developed by manually inspecting the
21
health states of machines, which increases the labor intensity and reduces the diagnosis
22
accuracy. Advanced signal processing methods [38-40] enable to help ensure which types of
23
Page 10
faults or where the faults happened in machines. However, these methods greatly rely on the
1
specialized knowledge that maintainers mostly lack in engineering scenarios. Furthermore, the
2
diagnosis results by signal processing methods are too specialized to be understood by the
3
machine users. Therefore, modern industrial applications prefer the fault diagnosis methods that
4
could automatically recognize the health states of machines.
5
With the help of machine learning theories, IFD is expected to achieve the above purpose [1,
6
5]. In the past period of IFD, some traditional machine learning theories, such as ANN and
7
SVM, are applied to machine fault diagnosis. The diagnosis process includes three steps [1], i.e.,
8
data collection, artificial feature extraction, and health state recognition, as shown in Fig. 2.
9
Each step will be detailed in the following subsections.
10
11
Fig. 2. Diagnosis process of IFD using traditional machine learning theories.
12
2.2. Step 1: Data collection
13
In the step of data collection, the sensors are mounted on machines to constantly collect
14
data. Different sensors are usually employed, such as vibration, acoustic emission, temperature,
15
and current transformer. Among them, vibration data are widely used in fault diagnosis of
16
Page 11
bearings [4, 41] and gearboxes [42, 43]. Acoustic emission data are potential to detect the
1
incipient faults and the deformation of bearings [44, 45] and gears [46-48], especially under the
2
low-speed operation conditions and low-frequency-noise environment. Instantaneous speed data
3
are commonly used in fault diagnosis of engines [49-51], which are strongly anti-interference.
4
Current data play an important role in fault diagnosis of electric-driven machines [52-54]. This
5
kind of data is easily collected just by using the current transformer, and does not include into
6
the running of machines. In addition, researchers discovered that the data from multi-source
7
sensors have complementary information, which could be fused to achieve higher diagnosis
8
accuracy than just using data from the individual sensor [55].
9
2.3. Step 2: Artificial feature extraction
10
Artificial feature extraction includes two steps. First, some commonly-used features, such as
11
time-domain features, frequency-domain features, and time-frequency-domain features, are
12
extracted from the collected data. These features contain the health information reflecting the
13
health states of machines. Second, feature selection methods, such as filters, wrappers, and
14
embedded methods, are used to select sensitive features to health states of machines from the
15
extracted features. It is beneficial to getting rid of the redundant information and further
16
improving the diagnosis results. These two steps are detailed as follows.
17
2.3.1. Feature extraction
18
The commonly-used features can be extracted from the time domain, the frequency domain
19
analysis, or the time-frequency domain. 1) The time-domain features can be divided into the
20
dimensional ones and the dimensionless ones. The former includes mean, standard deviation,
21
root amplitude, root mean square, peak value, etc., which are affected by the speed and the load
22
of machines. The later mostly includes shape indicator, skewness, kurtosis, crest indicator,
23
Page 12
clearance indicator, impulse indicator, etc., which are robust to the operation conditions of
1
machines [56, 57]. 2) The frequency-domain features are extracted from the frequency
2
spectrum, such as mean frequency, frequency center, root mean square frequency, standard
3
deviation frequency, etc., which are introduced in Ref. [56, 57]. They contain the information
4
that cannot found in the time-domain features. 3) The time-frequency-domain features, such as
5
energy entropy [56, 57], are usually extracted by wavelet transform (WT), wavelet package
6
transform (WPT) or empirical model decompose (EMD). These features are able to reflect
7
health states of machines under non-stationary operation conditions.
8
2.3.2. Feature selection
9
The extracted features from the time domain, the frequency domain, and the time-frequency
10
domain contain the redundant information. They may aggravate the computation cost, and even
11
result in the curse of dimensionality. To weaken this problem, some publications [58-65] select
12
sensitive features to the health states of machines from the collected features. They can be
13
divided into three categories, i.e., filters, wrappers, and embedded methods.
14
(1) Filter-based methods
15
Filters directly preprocess the collected features, which are independent to the training of
16
the classifier [58]. Some filters are briefly introduced as follows. 1) Relief [66] and Relief-F [67]
17
construct a relevant indicator to determine the sensitivity of features to the health states of
18
machines. 2) Information gain and gain ratio [68], from the information theory, are also two
19
commonly-used methods for feature selection. The features with the greater information gain
20
and the higher gain ratio would be selected to train diagnosis models and improve their
21
diagnosis results. 3) Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) [69] attempts to
22
select features subject to the maximal dissimilarity with each other. 4) Fisher score [70] is
23
Page 13
regarded as a distance metric to feature selection, which aims to select a feature that is able to
1
maximize the among-class distance, but minimize the in-class distance. 5) Distance evaluation
2
(DE) [71, 72] is used to select a feature set by the distance metric, in which the sensitive features
3
are subject to the small in-class distance and the large among-class distance.
4
(2) Wrapper-based methods
5
Different from filter-based methods, wrappers focus on the interaction of feature selection
6
with training classifiers [58]. In other words, the performance of classifiers is used to assess the
7
selected feature set. If the selected feature subset cannot produce the optimal classification
8
accuracy, another subset is reselected in the next iteration until the selected features enforce the
9
classifiers at the most favorable performance. Las Vegas wrapper (LVW) [73] is widely used to
10
select the features, in which the Las Vegas algorithm is employed to search for the feature
11
subset, and the error of the classifiers is considered as the metric to feature assessment.
12
(3) Embedded methods
13
Embedded methods integrate the feature selection into training the classifiers. Generally,
14
they impose the regularization terms on the optimization objects of the classifiers, and
15
automatically select the features once the training of classifiers is done [58]. Two regularization
16
terms are commonly considered. One is the L1 regularization [74], and the other one is the L2
17
regularization [75]. Both them can alleviate the over fitting that occurs in training with a small
18
amount of training samples. In contrast, the L1 term prefers to obtain the sparse parameters,
19
which is able to abandon redundant features in classification and further enforce the classifier to
20
achieve the high classification performance.
21
2.4. Step 3: Health state recognition
22
Health state recognition uses machine learning-based diagnosis models to establish the
23
Page 14
relationship between the selected features and the health states of machines. To achieve the
1
purpose, the diagnosis models are first trained with labeled samples. After that, the models are
2
able to recognize the health states of machines when the input samples are unlabeled. According
3
to the research popularity, we will briefly introduce four IFD approaches using traditional
4
machine learning in the following subsections.
5
2.4.1. Expert system-based approaches
6
(1) A brief introduction to expert system
7
The expert system is viewed as a method that can provide the expert-level diagnosis
8
knowledge to solve the diagnosis tasks of machines instead of huge human labor. The expert
9
system-based diagnosis models, as shown in Fig. 3, consist of five parts, i.e., the knowledge
10
base, the database, the inference engine, the user interface, and the explanation system [76].
11
Each part is briefly described as follows.

(2) Applications of expert system to machine fault diagnosis
11
According to different inference engines, expert system-based diagnosis models can be
12
divided into four categories, i.e. rule-based reasoning, fuzzy logic-based reasoning, neural
13
network-based reasoning, and case-based reasoning. Each part is reviewed as follows. 1) The
14
rule-based reasoning is used to manipulate diagnosis knowledge and then make decision by
15
designed rules [15, 77]. In the field of IFD, Krishnamurthi et al. [78] designed a rule-based
16
reasoning expert system for a Cincinnati Milacron 786 robot, which was one of the earliest
17
research in this field. The designed diagnosis shell really reduced the development time and
18
effort of diagnosis models in knowledge acquisition, application system generation, learning,
19
explanation. Gelgele et al. [79] employed IF-THEN rule to construct an expert system-based
20
diagnosis model for automotive engines. Furthermore, the rule-based reasoning was used for
21
fault diagnosis of hydraulic systems [80], rolling element bearings [81], and centrifugal pumps
22
[82]. Although the rule-based reasoning can establish the nonlinear mapping from the elected
23
Page 16
features to the health states, the reasoning efficiency drops with the increasing number of
1
designed rules for sophisticated machines. 2) The fuzzy logic-based reasoning introduces fuzzy
2
set theory into inference engine to describe the imprecise and non-numerical information [15,
3
77]. In IFD, Lee et al. [83] designed a fuzzy reasoning system for power systems, which was
4
one of the earliest work about the applications of fuzzy logic-based reasoning. The proposed
5
system included four parts, i.e., Meta inference system, expert system for hybrid diagnosis,
6
expert system for the diagnosis of substations, and expert system for the diagnosis of
7
transmission network, which improved efficiency and reliability of the fault diagnosis process.
8
Liu et al. [84] used fuzzy multi-attribute group decision making method to construct expert
9
system-based diagnosis models. Wu et al. [85] employed the fuzzy-logic inference to recognize
10
the health states of scooter engines. Berredjem et al. [86] applied fuzzy expert system to fault
11
diagnosis of bearings and achieved high diagnosis accuracy. The performance of fuzzy logic-
12
based reasoning is related to the fuzzy dataset, but it is difficult to be captured. Therefore, such
13
reasoning commonly has low learning ability, which may reduce the diagnosis accuracy. 3) The
14
neural network-based reasoning inherits the capabilities of learning, association, and memory of
15
neural networks [15, 77]. Wu et al. [87, 88] respectively used the probability neural network and
16
the generalized regression neural network to construct expert system-based diagnosis models for
17
internal combustion engines. Hajnayeb et al. [89] employed multi-layer perceptron neural
18
network to construct the inference engine and infer the relationship between the collected data
19
and the health states of bearings. Jayaswal et al. [90] combined ANN and fuzzy rules to
20
construct expert system-base diagnosis models for bearings. The neural network-based
21
reasoning needs to acquire diagnosis knowledge from sufficient training data, which is difficult
22
to be met in engineering scenarios. In addition, such reasoning cannot clearly explain the
23
Page 17
reasoning process and the physical meaning of the saved knowledge due to the black box of the
1
neural network. 4) The case-based reasoning attempts to solve specialized problems according
2
to the solutions of similar existing problems [15]. Vingerhoeds et al. [91] used the case-based
3
reasoning to incorporate the knowledge and experience from both train manufacturers and
4
railway companies for on-line fault diagnosis. Varma et al. [92] presented a case-based
5
reasoning system for fault diagnosis of locomotive by using on-board fault messages. Wu et al.
6
[93] developed an expert system for fault diagnosis of modern commercial aircraft, which was
7
designed by the case-based reasoning and the fuzzy logic. Vong et al. [94] constructed a
8
computer-aided diagnosis system based on the case-based reasoning and the kernel k-means for
9
the automotive engine ignition system.
10
The expert system-based diagnosis models represent the diagnosis knowledge from experts
11
as the inference algorithm to automatically recognize the health states of machines. However,
12
the performance of the diagnosis models greatly relies on the expert knowledge, which is
13
difficult to be acquired and expressed. The incorrect and incomplete knowledge may reduce the
14
diagnosis accuracy. Furthermore, the expert system lacks the self-learning capability so that the
15
diagnosis knowledge base is difficult to be expanded and corrected.

(2) How to construct deep learning-based diagnosis models subject to special issues in the
13
revolution of big data?
14
With the revolution of big data, two special issues come to bring negative effects on the IFD
15
using deep learning theories, i.e., imbalanced health states and analytics for data stream. 1)
16
Imbalanced distribution in health states of machines is a common phenomenon in engineering
17
scenarios. For example, the data collected from the healthy state are far more sufficient than
18
those from the faults. If the imbalanced data are used to train the deep learning-based diagnosis
19
models, the decision boundary of the models might be enforced to shift towards the health states
20
with minority of instances, thus the diagnosis accuracy would be reduced. To overcome the
21
issue, the cost sensitive learning may help construct diagnosis models subject to imbalanced
22
health states. In addition, ensemble learning, such as Adaboost and XGboost, is expected to
23
Page 65
improve the performance of deep learning-based diagnosis models when combined with the
1
resampling strategies. 2) The monitoring data stream is regard as the increasingly-enlarged data
2
with the continuous time series. By analyzing that, IFD is possible to provide the real-time
3
diagnosis results. Such issue has been concerned by the researchers for years, but the unreliable
4
data transmission and the bandwidth limitations prevent the monitoring data stream from
5
arriving the destination in an unbroken sequence. Furthermore, the inefficient computation
6
capability impedes the success of data stream analytics. As a result, the IFD using deep learning
7
is just implemented based on the off-line historical data. Fortunately, the monitoring data stream
8
is able to be collected and efficiently handled with the advent of IoT, broadband internet, and
9
cloud computing. Therefore, the on-line IFD is encouraged to be developed to make real-time
10
decisions on the incipient anomaly or the sudden faults of machines. The incremental learning is
11
expected to facilitate the on-line IFD using deep learning. Furthermore, the lifelong learning
12
may promote deep learning-based diagnosis models to constantly acquire the diagnosis
13
knowledge from the monitoring data stream.
14
(3) How to protect the performance of transfer learning-based diagnosis models from the
15
negative transfer in engineering scenarios?
16
The successes of transfer learning are subject to the assumption of related health
17
information across multiple diagnosis tasks. If the assumption is invalid, the negative transfer
18
may happen to reduce the transfer performance of the transfer learning-based diagnosis models
19
by using the diagnosis knowledge from the source domain. Two reasons may cause the negative
20
transfer. 1) It is possible to collect data from multiple source domains to match a common target
21
domain, but the health information contained in these source domains is not all related to the
22
that in the target domain in engineering scenarios. For example, the data from motors with
23
Page 66
different specifications can be collected to form multiple source domains. Some of them could
1
provide positive diagnosis knowledge for a generator with similar physical construction to the
2
motors, but not all of them. Consequently, it confuses the researchers to select the optimal one
3
and guarantee the performance of the transfer learning-based diagnosis models. Therefore, it is
4
necessary to develop metrics to cross-domain transferability, which may help select the relevant
5
source domains. Furthermore, GAN could help generate fake high-transferability data to extend
6
the available data for IFD using transfer learning. 2) The constructed transfer learning-based
7
diagnosis models are incapable to extract the related health information. According to Section
8
4.3, several approaches can be used in IFD, but the transfer performance of them is different for
9
a given transfer scenario due to diverse performance ceilings. To select the optimal one and
10
guarantee the transfer success, it must take much time by experimental trials. For this issue, the
11
architecture of learning to transfer is expected to automatically select the optimal approaches
12
with the highest performance based on the historical knowledge. Furthermore, with the help of
13
transitive transfer learning, the diagnosis knowledge of the source domain may be reused in the
14
target domain if the negative transfer inevitably happens in engineering scenarios.
15
(4) How to improve the interpretability of the deep learning-based diagnosis models?
16
Although there are state-of-the-art achievements of deep learning-based diagnosis models,
17
an open issue of black box for deep hierarchical networks still confuses the academic
18
researchers. It is difficult to acquire how these models learn the diagnosis knowledge from the
19
monitoring data. As a result, the diagnosis models are constructed by experimental trials once
20
and once again rather than the strictly theoretical background. To bridge the gap, two research
21
interests are recommended to be concerned. 1) The deep learning-based diagnosis models are
22
trained by minimizing empirical risk, which really lacks rigorous theory. As a result, the
23
Page 67
physical meanings of them are difficult to be interpretable. The statistical learning theories, such
1
as SVM and PGM, have rigorous theory grounds, which promote to constructed diagnosis
2
models with easily-understood model parameters, features, and diagnosis results. Therefore, it is
3
still worthy to investigate statistical learning in IFD with the revolution of big data. 2) The
4
process of learning features through deep learning is similar to the filtering process. Therefore,
5
the adaptive filter theory is beneficial to analyzing the physical meanings of deep learning-based
6
diagnosis models. In addition, the visualization technologies, such as maximizing the activation
7
and feature inversion, are expected to visually express what the diagnosis models learn from the
8
input data. According to the above research, the interpretability results are helpful to construct
9
the deep learning-based diagnosis models with the optimal architectures reasonably.
